body:
I see all my curl-using programs experience major delays/stucks after 8.6.0->8.7.1 upgrade on linux (win & mac seems ok).
I'll see if I can debug them a bit.

Upd.:
All programs hang with this trace and after 2-5 mins continue normally.
```
(gdb) bt
#0  0x00007f1d3e65023e in __GI___select (nfds=16, readfds=0x7ffe250f0310, writefds=0x7ffe250f0390, exceptfds=0x7ffe250f0410, timeout=0x7ffe250f0300) at ../sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/select.c:69
#1  0x00007f1d3f261f88 in Curl_poll.part.0 () from badger.curl.libcurl-8.7.1.so
#2  0x00007f1d3f24f86a in multi_wait.part () from badger.curl.libcurl-8.7.1.so
#3  0x00007f1d3f24fd5a in curl_multi_poll () from badger.curl.libcurl-8.7.1.so
#4  0x00007f1d3f215e5e in curl_easy_perform () from badger.curl.libcurl-8.7.1.so
#5  0x00007f1d3f9aae84 in download_file(std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&, std::filesystem::__cxx11::path const&, long) ()
```

Build is kinda custom, maybe I have issues with it.
Without being able to reproduce this locally, this feels next to impossible to fix.

Absolutely agree.  I guess this was more a a cry of has anyone else seen this before, or have any hunches.

I'll try building curl on my lowest machine and seeing if I can make it replicate there.

Just as another data point, we are also seeing some timeouts in Debian's buildd network.

https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=curl&arch=amd64&ver=8.7.1-5%2Bexp1&stamp=1715630000&raw=0
https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=curl&arch=amd64&ver=8.7.1-5%2Bexp1&stamp=1715628225&raw=0
https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=curl&arch=i386&ver=8.7.1-5%2Bexp1&stamp=1715627959&raw=0
https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=curl&arch=arm64&ver=8.7.1-5%7Ebpo12%2B1&stamp=1715892677&raw=0
https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=curl&arch=arm64&ver=8.7.1-5%7Ebpo12%2B1&stamp=1715749009&raw=0

I also spent the day today rebuilding the package locally, and these tests also eventually timeout: 226, 350, 351, 352, 353, 354, 362, 401, 408, 409, 520, 525, 533, 534, 593, 661, 1028, 1055, 1057, 1096, 1107, 1108, 1114, 1149, 1206, 1224, 1226, 1380, 1381, 1383, 1384, 1386, 1390, 1393.

As far as I can see, they are all ftp-related. The timeouts only started appearing after we enabled parallel tests.
We had a fail in automated CI again, and it's FTP-related. You may be onto something!

The tests that we've seen fail are: 136 137 138 139 337 340 1062 1086 1091 1096 1103 1107 1108 1137 1149. Only three match, but if the bug/race is in the FTP harness and there's a lot of tests, that's not a surprise.

I think I'm just going to try filtering out the FTP tests and seeing if that stops them entirely, or if different tests fail then.

After doing some bisecting, the timeouts started to appear on f6513b998266dfe91ef5c52f67c416cc0a0de0a2, which fixed #12002. This might be wrong since the timeouts are somewhat infrequent on my machine, but it seems like a good starting point.

I'll try to hack on this code for a while, but I'm not sure I'll be able to fix it :^)

All the Debian FTP failure logs linked above have a failure mode like this:
```
=== Start of file trace235
 20:49:03.766312 == Info:   Trying 127.0.0.1:43041...
 20:49:03.766386 == Info: Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 43041
 20:51:03.926167 == Info: server response timeout
 20:51:03.926323 == Info: Closing connection
=== End of file trace235
```
i.e. the socket is open, client can connect, but nothing responds and the test times out. This is the most common failure mode I've seen with parallel testing failures recently. It does seems like there's another race condition that #12002 didn't fix. I'm guessing the *previous* test would have had some interesting logs that would have given some clues as to how the system got into the state, since the ftp and socket servers don't seem to be writing any logs in the failing tests. That's a clue that implies that something in the server processes has gone out of sync again.

body: @bagder: a small correction: the issue isn't that one test fails, the issue appears to be that the FTP tests are unstable.

@rossburton have you tried the current `master`. I did some stabilizing in FTP data connection handling, which seems to have improved our CI "greenness". But maybe I am halucinating like the machines.

> @rossburton have you tried the current `master`. I did some stabilizing in FTP data connection handling, which seems to have improved our CI "greenness". But maybe I am halucinating like the machines.

I have not, but if you can point to specific commits I can apply them and see what happens.

> have you tried the current master. I did some stabilizing in FTP data connection handling, which seems to have improved our CI "greenness". But maybe I am halucinating like the machines.

I feel like the failure rate is lower now, but I can still see some failing tests occasionally. I tested on 282b9fe8f, and after running the test suite a few times test case 587 failed.

```
 527: protocol FAILED!
 There was no content at all in the file log/19/server.input.
 Server glitch? Total curl failure? Returned: 125
```

>  I'm guessing the previous test would have had some interesting logs that would have given some clues as to how the system got into the state

I assume that _previous test_ does not relate to the numerical order. Is there a way to figure out what test ran just before the one that failed? I can try to send logging information.
Tests are normally run in numerically-increasing order, unless specific test numbers are given on the command-line or the -j -R or --repeat options are given to runtests.

> Tests are normally run in numerically-increasing order, unless specific test numbers are given on the command-line or the -j -R or --repeat options are given to runtests.

Yes, I'm using `-j56`. I assumed that the tests were only failing with parallel testing enabled, so I didn't even try to reproduce without it. I'll run them a few more times to see if I hit any more failures.

I can be tricky to find the "previous" test with -j, since previous in this
regard refers to the previous test run by the same test process/runner, which
isn't really logged. By specifying -k you can keep some previous log files
around and look at the time stamps but you still might not get enough
interesting information.
